body:
Currently, we have this requirement:

| # | Description | Level |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **3.3.4** | Verify that if the value of a cookie is not meant to be accessible to client-side scripts (such as a session token), the cookie must have the 'HttpOnly' attribute set and the same value (e. g. session token) must only be transferred to the client via the 'Set-Cookie' header field. | 2 |

There are apparently new `__Http-` and `__Host-Http-` prefixes for `HttpOnly` cookies, which protects the cookie from being overwritten by client-side JS code. Shall we require this usage somehow in this requirement?

Caveat: there is no `__Secure-Http-` prefix for some reason.

comments.body:
Description from [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie)

> __Host-Http-: Cookies with names starting with __Host-Http- must be set with the Secure flag by a secure page (HTTPS) and must have the HttpOnly attribute set to prove that they were set via the Set-Cookie header. In addition, they also have the same restrictions as __Host--prefixed cookies. This combination yields a cookie that is as close as can be to treating the origin as a security boundary while at the same time ensuring developers and server operators know that its scope is limited to HTTP requests.

It is at the moment with 65% of global coverage: https://caniuse.com/mdn-http_headers_set-cookie_http_host-http_prefixes

What we have at the moment:

  * `__Host-` prefix is required (v5.0.0-3.3.3)
  * `HttpOnly` is required if the cookie is not meant to be accessible for JavaScript (v5.0.0-3.3.4)

What it could give extra: if there is a browser-side JavaScript execution possibility for the attacker, then it is not possible to (over)write the cookie with the name prefix `__Host-Http-` (or `__Http-` but we require `__Host-` to be used anyway).

As `__Host-Http-` to have any impact, it requires malicious JavaScript execution in the same-origin scope as pre-condition, then I'm not convinced that in practice it solves or mitigates any security problems. ~~Definitely not worth a level 2 requirement. If there is consensus that it is needed, then maybe for level 3, into the same requirement.~~

edit: thinking more about it, it has enough impact to be part of the current requirement.

This has come up on my radar as well. I don't think we want to edit or add a new requirement, but what about adding it as a note somehow? 

Folks have used cookie clobbering to do session fixation and similar in a lot of legacy attacks via XSS. Very surgical.

> If malicious JS execution is already possible, does this really help?”

Most often this is no. But sometimes yes, particularly when:

- session binding is strict
- privileged actions require fresh cookies
- auth cookies are rotated or bound to IP/device

> This has come up on my radar as well. I don't think we want to edit or add a new requirement, but what about adding it as a note somehow?

Yes, I agree with @elarlang  and @jmanico  analysis. Adding a note at some point could be a good choice for that.

So the action plan here is:
* For the next patch release, we can add a note to the section text to mention the possibility
* For the next minor or major release, we'll modify the requirement as we feel is correct at the time
For reference, see [new wording](https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-browser-based-apps/pull/112) of the OAuth for Browser based apps document.
